![Concern about AI among adults under 30 climbed from 31% in 2021 to 55% in 2026, while their excitement fell from 25% to 11%. Chart from [Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/08/18/young-adults-in-the-us-are-increasingly-wary-of-ai-concerned-it-will-take-jobs/).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[Colleen McClain](https://www.pewresearch.org/staff/colleen-mcclain/) and [Eugenie Park](https://www.pewresearch.org/staff/eugenie-park/) at [Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/) report that American concern about AI is still rising, and that adults under 30 are the group whose concern has kept climbing instead of levelling off after 2023. The survey covered 3,488 U.S. adults from June 22 to 28, 2026, through the Center's [American Trends Panel](https://www.pewresearch.org/the-american-trends-panel/), with the [questionnaire](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/08/SR_26.08.19_young-adults-ai_questionnaire.pdf), [topline](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/08/SR_26.08.19_young-adults-ai_topline.pdf), and [methodology](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/08/SR_26.08.19_young-adults-ai_methodology.pdf) published alongside it.

What the survey finds:

- **Most Americans lean concerned.** 52% say the increased use of AI in daily life makes them more concerned than excited, up from 37% in 2021. 9% are more excited than concerned, and 37% feel both equally.

- **Under-30s cross a majority for the first time.** 55% of adults aged 18 to 29 are more concerned than excited, up from 31% in 2021 and 47% a year ago. Their excitement fell from 25% to 11% over the same period.

- **The older groups rose earlier, by 2023.** Their 2026 readings are 51% for ages 30 to 49, 47% for 50 to 64, and 59% for 65 and older, against 48%, 59%, and 61% in 2023.

- **Expected job losses are up seven points.** 71% think AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S. over the next 20 years, against 64% in 2024. 5% expect more jobs, 10% expect no real difference, and 14% are unsure.

- **Young adults now match ages 30 to 64.** 73% of under-30s expect fewer jobs, up from 61% in 2024. They are now level with ages 30 to 49 (74%) and 50 to 64 (72%). Adults 65 and older are lowest at 63%.

Pew also cites its earlier work on the same age group. Adults under 30 are the group most likely to say AI will be [bad for society and bad for them personally](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2026/06/17/how-opinions-and-use-of-ai-differ-by-age/), and to expect it to [make connection and creativity harder to come by](https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2025/09/17/ai-impact-on-people-society-appendix/ps_2024-9-15_ai-and-its-impact_a-08/). Most of them use chatbots, and they are [about as likely to say the tools hurt their own creativity as help it](https://www.pewresearch.org/chart/unlike-older-americans-adults-under-30-are-just-as-likely-to-think-chatbots-hurt-their-creativity-as-help-it/).

## My Notes

- **Expectations moved most where employment actually fell.** Under-30s' expectation of fewer jobs rose 12 points since 2024, ahead of 8 points for ages 30 to 49 and 3 points for 50 to 64. The payroll data is ordered the same way. [The AI Entry-Level Jobs Effect Isn't Fading](/posts/20260628-ai-entry-level-jobs/) put employment for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations down about 3.8% a year, ages 31 to 34 down 1.7%, and ages 35 to 40 growing at 2%. [AI and Job Postings: From Destruction to Creation?](/posts/20260713-ai-and-job-postings-from-destruction-to-creation/) found the software-posting rebound going to senior roles. Adults 65 and older rose 5 points, and the payroll data does not cover them.

- **Concern is falling among 50-to-64-year-olds.** Concern among adults aged 50 to 64 peaked at 59% in 2023 and has come down every year since, to 47% in 2026. They are now the least concerned of the four age groups, and the only one whose concern is falling. Their excitement stayed flat at 7% to 8% across those years. Pew does not say why.
  - **Only the three-year fall clears sampling error.** Pew's [methodology](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/08/SR_26.08.19_young-adults-ai_methodology.pdf) puts 902 respondents in this age band, at a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 points. The 12-point drop since 2023 is well outside that. The three single-year steps of 3, 4, and 5 points each fall inside it, so "falling every year" describes the point estimates rather than three separate declines.
  - **Their expectation of job loss barely moved.** Their 3-point rise since 2024 is the smallest of any working-age group, and it fits the payroll data. The series in [The AI Entry-Level Jobs Effect Isn't Fading](/posts/20260628-ai-entry-level-jobs/) comes from the Stanford Digital Economy Lab and ADP [Canaries Dashboard](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/project/indicators/canaries-dashboard/). The dashboard has employment growing about 2% a year for workers aged 35 to 40 while the 22-to-25 cohort contracts about 3.8%. The dashboard's age bands stop short of 50 to 64, so that is the direction of the gradient and not a reading for this group.
  - **Direct experience may be lowering their concern.** Chatbot use in this group rose from 25% to 42% between 2024 and 2026, per Pew's [February 2026 age report](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2026/06/17/how-opinions-and-use-of-ai-differ-by-age/). On that survey's separate positive-or-negative question they gave AI's effect on society the highest positive rating of any age group, 18%. The conjecture has a clear counterexample: under-30s use chatbots most of all, 66%, and are the most concerned, so exposure by itself does not lower concern.
